doc.title: David Spinozza interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, NY, September 27, 2025

title: Turning down work, session lengths and being as good as your last call
summary: He explains declining some producers, three-hour bookings with overtime options and the fear of losing calls from contractors.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: After you had done that for a bunch of years, did you ever turn anything down because of the kind of music it was?

Not because of the kind of – I turned it down sometimes because if I didn’t like the producer or the arranger, if I thought they were like taskmasters or something that I didn’t agree with I would turn it down. Once I was established and was making enough money to say no, sometimes I would turn it down based on how much stress I thought the session was going to be you know.
And the average session was four hours a day?

Usually three hours, they would book it as three hours with a possible 20 or three hours with a possible 40, there was always this possible thing. They would say that so that you wouldn’t book something right away. Like if you have a 10-1 they didn’t want you to have a 1:30 booked somewhere because just in case they needed the overtime. So they would book sessions in three hour increments with a plus 20 or a plus 40.
What would cause a studio musician to stop getting called?
You would stop being called because the last session you played on you didn’t rise to the occasion.
Yeah. I mean to me you’re always as good as your last call. And everybody lived in fear of that, of like oh my God here I couldn’t sight read this thing or I was out of tune or whatever it was.
And so the contractors would like –

And the contractor would know and if the producers complained to the contractor, “I don’t want to see that guy again” or whatever, that would be it. That’s why it was so stressful because you really were only as good as your last phone call. You were never sure there was going to be another session. In fact there’s a joke about it. There’s two musicians or something, they’re talking one day. And this one musician says to the other musician, “Did you hear last week I played a score for a movie?” And then the other one said, “Did you hear I met Marilyn Monroe? I’m sleeping with Marilyn Monroe.” And he said, “Oh, by the way,” he said, “did you hear I played this one session and I was a little out of tune.” “Yeah I heard about that.” That’s kind of what it was like.
